claim: Microbial populations can exhibit diverse individualistic behaviors and yet can engage in collective migratory patterns with a spatially sorted arrangement of phenotypes.
source: Microbial populations can exhibit diverse individualistic behaviors, and yet can engage in collective migratory patterns with a spatially sorted arrangement of phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about microbial populations.

claim: The drift velocities of individual bacteria decrease from the back to the front during group migration, despite the constant migrating speed of the group.
source: despite the constant migrating speed of a group, the drift velocities of individual bacteria decrease from the back to the front.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The decreasing profile of drift velocities implies the spatial modulation of individual run-and-tumble random motions.
source: we showed that this decreasing profile of drift velocities implies the spatial modulation of individual run-and-tumble random motions
evidence: This is derived from Langevin-type modeling framework analysis as stated in the abstract.

claim: The spatial modulation of individual run-and-tumble random motions enables the bacterial population to migrate as a pushed wave front.
source: this decreasing profile of drift velocities implies the spatial modulation of individual run-and-tumble random motions, and enables the bacterial population to migrate as a pushed wave front.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Langevin-type modeling framework stated in the abstract.

claim: The pushed wave front can help a diverse population to stay in a tight group.
source: Theoretical analysis and stochastic simulations further predicted that the pushed wave front can help a diverse population to stay in a tight group
evidence: This is predicted by theoretical analysis and stochastic simulations as stated in the abstract.

claim: Diverse individuals perform the same type of mean reverting processes around centers orderly aligned by their chemotactic abilities.
source: while diverse individuals perform the same type of mean reverting processes around centers orderly aligned by their chemotactic abilities.
evidence: This is predicted by theoretical analysis and stochastic simulations as stated in the abstract.

claim: The mechanism about the emergence of orderly collective migration from diverse individuals is experimentally demonstrated by titration of bacterial chemoreceptor abundance.
source: This mechanism about the emergence of orderly collective migration from diverse individuals is experimentally demonstrated by titration of bacterial chemoreceptor abundance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Collective group migration is ubiquitous in living systems, such as navigation, foraging, and range expansion.
source: Collective group migration, as an important class of coordinated behaviors, is ubiquitous in living systems, such as navigation, foraging, and range expansion (Krause et al., 2002; Partridge, 1982; Sumpter, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the presence of individual heterogeneity, the migrating group often exhibits spatially ordered arrangements of phenotypes.
source: In the presence of individual heterogeneity, the migrating group often exhibits spatially ordered arrangements of phenotypes (Krause et al., 2002; Parrish and Edelstein-Keshet, 1999; Partridge, 1982; Sumpter, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In animal group migration, individual behavioral abilities would result in social hierarchy, which further drives the spatial arrangement in a coordinated group.
source: In animal group migration, individual behavioral abilities (e.g., directional sensitivity) would result in social hierarchy, which further drives the spatial arrangement in a coordinated group (Couzin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Spatial arrangements can lead to different costs and benefits for the individuals participating in the group migration.
source: At the same time, spatial arrangements can lead to different costs and benefits for the individuals participating in the group migration (Krause, 1994; Parrish and Edelstein-Keshet, 1999; Partridge, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Participating individuals must follow disciplinary rules to organize themselves into coordinated patterns while on the move, which requires complex computational abilities to interact with the group and the environment.
source: Participating individuals must follow disciplinary rules to organize themselves into coordinated patterns while on the move, which requires complex computational abilities to interact with the group and the environment (Couzin and Krause, 2003; Couzin et al., 2002; Vicsek and Zafeiris, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Escherichia coli can exhibit both individualistic behaviors and collective migratory patterns.
source: The chemotactic microbe, Escherichia coli, provides a simple model to address the emergence of collective decision-making among diverse population, as it can exhibit both individualistic behaviors (Dufour et al., 2016; Frankel et al., 2014; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Waite et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2018) and collective migratory patterns (Adler, 1966a; Fu et al., 2018; Keller and Segel, 1971a, Wolfe and Berg, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Individual E. coli cells perform run-and-tumble random motions by spontaneously switching the rotating direction of flagella.
source: Individual cells perform run-and-tumble random motions by spontaneously switching the rotating direction of flagella (Berg, 2004; Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: E. coli cells can facilitate the chemotaxis pathway to control the switching frequency to bias their motions toward their favorable direction along the chemoattractant gradient.
source: These cells can facilitate the chemotaxis pathway to control the switching frequency to bias their motions toward their favorable direction along the chemoattractant gradient, where the efficiency to climb the gradient is defined as the chemotactic ability (χ) (Celani and Vergassola, 2010; Dufour et al., 2014; de Gennes, 2004; Si et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The chemotactic abilities of individual cells exhibit substantial phenotypic heterogeneity even for the clonal bacterial population.
source: In addition, the chemotactic abilities of individual cells exhibit substantial phenotypic heterogeneity even for the clonal bacterial population, which diversifies the chemotactic response to identical signals (Spudich and Koshland, 1976; Waite et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The E. coli population can migrate as a coherent group by following a self-generated attractant gradient, via consumption of the whole population.
source: Despite the stochastic solitary behavior and variations in phenotypic ability, the E. coli population can migrate as a coherent group by following a self-generated attractant gradient, via consumption of the whole population (Adler, 1966a; Saragosti et al., 2011; Wolfe and Berg, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The migratory group forms a stable pattern of phenotypes sorted by their chemotactic abilities.
source: The migratory group form a stable pattern of phenotypes sorted by their chemotactic abilities (Figure 1A), which is believed to maintain phenotypic diversity in the group (Fu et al., 2018; Waite et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Behavior modulation helps migrating bacteria to maintain a consistent group.
source: Although a previous study showed that behavior modulation helps migrating bacteria to maintain a consistent group (Saragosti et al., 2011), how individuals with phenotypic variations manage to determine their relative positions in the group remains to be determined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The bacterial density profile is stable in the moving coordinate z=x−VGt.
source: Bacterial density profile ρz is stable (black solid line) in the moving coordinate z=x − VGt.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with experimental data.

claim: Cells at the back of the group tended to run forward, compared with cells in other regions.
source: Sample runs of bacteria aligned by their initial positions (black dots) from the three regions (defined by colored regions in B) showed that cells at the back of the group tended to run forward, compared with cells in other regions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with experimental data.

claim: The exponential distributions of forward runs and backward runs suggested the increasing efficiency of runs from the back to the front.
source: The exponential distributions of forward runs (solid lines) and backward runs (dashed lines) suggested the increasing efficiency of runs from the back to the front.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with experimental data.

claim: VD(z) crossing with the average group velocity VG implied that bacteria perform mean reversion motions.
source: VD (z) crossing with the average group velocity VG (black dashed line), implied that bacteria perform mean reversion motions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and is an inference from the data.

claim: The time evolution of the average position of cells starting from the back, middle, and front of the migration group confirmed the reversion behavior.
source: The time evolution of the average position (z, solid lines) of cells starting from the back, middle, and front of the migration group (color code was defined in B) confirmed the reversion behavior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G with experimental data.

claim: The group velocity VG was constant over time, VG∼3.0μm/s.
source: Because the group velocity VG=〈Δxi(t)/Δt〉 was constant over time, VG∼3.0μm/s (Appendix 1—figure 2)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The average instantaneous velocity, VI(z)=⟨Δxi(z)/Δt⟩, was constant along the density profile ρ(z).
source: We first checked that the average instantaneous velocity, VI(z)=⟨Δxi(z)/Δt⟩, was constant along the density profile ρ(z) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The runs in the front were longer but distributed more uniformly in terms of the directionality, whereas the runs in the back were shorter but more oriented toward the group migration direction.
source: Comparing the sample events initiated from the back (b), middle (m), and front (f) of the migration group, we observed that the runs in the front were longer but distributed more uniformly in terms of the directionality, whereas the runs in the back were shorter but more oriented toward the group migration direction (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C and Appendix 1—figure 3A, B.

claim: The statistics of run length (and duration) displayed exponential distributions with the means for the direction of group migration longer than those for the opposite direction.
source: Quantitatively, the statistics of run length (and duration) displayed exponential distributions with the means for the direction of group migration longer than those for the opposite direction (Figure 1D, Appendix 1—figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D and Appendix 1—figure 3C.

claim: Cells in the back showed greater directional persistence toward the migration direction.
source: We also confirmed that cells in the back showed greater directional persistence toward the migration direction (Appendix 1—figure 4A–C), as (Saragosti et al., 2011) reported previously.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section, shown in Appendix 1—figure 4A–C, and supported by citation.

claim: The bacteria in the back run more effectively toward the direction of group migration than those in the front.
source: All these results suggested that the bacteria in the back run more effectively toward the direction of group migration than those in the front.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in the Results section.

claim: The mean reverting behavior results in sub-diffusion of individuals relative to the group.
source: Such mean reverting process also results in sub-diffusion of individuals relative to the group (Appendix 1—figure 3F), for which the mean square displacement (MSD) is constrained over time (Appendix 1—figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 3F and 3G.

claim: The expected drift velocity VD(z) represents the drift velocity driven by the external stimuli.
source: Since the run duration is explicitly modulated by the gradient of chemoattractant gz and is dependent on the chemotactic ability χ , VD(z)=χgz represents the drift velocity driven by the external stimuli (Celani and Vergassola, 2010; de Gennes, 2004; Dufour et al., 2014; Si et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The Langevin-type model describes bacterial motions as an active Brownian particle driven by the expected drift velocity VD and a random force: dx=VDdt+ϵdW.
source: To understand how the spatially structured profile of the drift velocity VD impacts on the group migration, we first adopted a Langevin-type model that describes bacterial motions as an active Brownian particle driven by the expected drift velocity VD and a random force: dx=VDdt+ϵdW (Berg, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: The stochastic description of bacterial motions has been proven equivalent to the classic Keller-Segel (KS) model that described the population dynamics of bacterial chemotactic group migration.
source: Such a stochastic description of bacterial motions has been proven equivalent to the classic Keller-Segel (KS) model that described the population dynamics of bacterial chemotactic group migration (Keller and Segel, 1971a, Rosen, 1973).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: These two 'forces' constrain the random motions of individuals in an effective potential well U(z).
source: These two 'forces' constrain the random motions of individuals in an effective potential well Uz (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The perceived gradient g(z) is deduced from S(z), which is further calculated from the experimentally measured density profile.
source: The perceived gradient g(z) (blue line) is deduced from S(z), which is further calculated from the experimentally measured density profile (Appendix 1—figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2 caption and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The perceived gradient g(z) is almost linear in the main part of the wave profile.
source: Since the perceived gradient gz is almost linear in the main part of the wave profile, we approximated it by gz≈g0+g1z (Figure 2B, dashed line)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Behind the balanced position, cells experience a pushed force to catch up the group.
source: Behind the balanced position, cells experience a pushed force to catch up the group.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the model.

claim: Cells would start to fall back once they exceed the balanced position, where the driving force becomes negative.
source: Cells would start to fall back once they exceed the balanced position, where the driving force becomes negative.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the model.

claim: The decreasing profile of the driving force enables cells to perform mean reverting behaviors around the balanced position.
source: Therefore, the decreasing profile of the driving force enable cells to perform mean reverting behaviors around the balanced position.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the model.

claim: The expected rate that cells tend to revert back to the balanced position is defined by the slope of the spatially dependent driving force, r=χg1.
source: In addition, the expected rate that cells tend to revert back to the balanced position is defined by the slope of the spatially dependent driving force, r=χg1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The OU model has an equivalent form, known as the Fokker-Planck equation (Equation S19) which describes the spatial-temporal dynamics of cell density distribution.
source: The OU model (Equation 1) which describes the single-cell stochastic motions has an equivalent form, known as the Fokker-Planck equation (Equation S19) which describes the spatial-temporal dynamics of cell density distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a mathematical relationship.

claim: The effective driving force has a negative slope (g1<0).
source: From the solution, we noted that the effective driving force, as well as the drift velocity, has a negative slope (g1<0).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the model solution.

claim: The decreasing profile of the drift velocity suggests that the leading front of the group migrates as a pushed wave front.
source: The decreasing profile of the drift velocity suggests that the leading front of the group migrates as a pushed wave front (Gandhi et al., 2016; van Saarloos, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: As a key feature of the pushed wave, the leading front of the group drops parabolically, which is much faster than that of diffusion front.
source: As a key feature of the pushed wave, the leading front of the group drops parabolically, which is much faster than that of diffusion front.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a characteristic of pushed waves.

claim: The pushed wave leads to a tight density profile of group migration for a single phenotype population.
source: This further leads to a tight density profile of group migration for a single phenotype population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a consequence of the pushed wave.

claim: Given a monotonically decreasing profile of perceived gradient g(z), the driving force that each phenotypic individual experiences exhibits the same spatial dependency with the slopes depend on the intrinsic phenotypic properties of each phenotype ri=χig1.
source: Given a monotonically decreasing profile of perceived gradient gz , the driving force that each phenotypic individual experiences exhibits the same spatial dependency with the slopes depend on the intrinsic phenotypic properties of each phenotype ri=χig1 .
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an extension of the model to diverse phenotypes.

claim: The balanced positions z0 of the diverse phenotypes are orderly arranged.
source: This monotonic dependency means that the balanced positions z0 of the diverse phenotypes are orderly arranged.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a consequence of the monotonic dependency.

claim: Each phenotypic population migrates at a constant speed VG, following the moving gradient g(z).
source: By the stochastic Langevin-type model with phenotypic diversity in chemotactic ability, we first confirmed that each phenotypic population migrates at a constant speed VG , following the moving gradient gz (see supplementary text).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by supplementary text.

claim: The density profiles of cells with different χi follow the same shape but are spatially orderly aligned.
source: The density profiles of cells with different χi follow the same shape but are spatially orderly aligned (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The balanced positions z0,i of different phenotypes increase with their chemotactic abilities χi.
source: As predicted by the OU model, the balanced positions z0,i of different phenotypes increase with their chemotactic abilities χi (Figure 2E, black line)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The standard deviation (σi) of the density profiles decreases with χi.
source: while the standard deviation (σi) of the density profiles decreases with χi (Figure 2E, blue line).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Under the spatially decreasing driving force, cells with phenotypic diversity perform the same type of mean reverting processes with spatially ordered mean positions.
source: Therefore, under the spatially decreasing driving force, cells with phenotypic diversity perform the same type of mean reverting processes with spatially ordered mean positions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the model.

claim: Each phenotypic subpopulation propagates as a pushed wave front.
source: By close examination of the density profile, we found that each phenotypic subpopulation propagates as a pushed wave front.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the model.

claim: Simulation reveals a pushed wave front for the combination of these subpopulations with different chemotactic abilities.
source: We further calculated the total density profile of the entire migratory group with Gaussian distribution of chemotactic abilities under a decreasing linear gradient. Simulation reveals a pushed wave front for the combination of these subpopulations with different chemotactic abilities (Figure 2F, insert).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F insert.

claim: The width of the entire group maintains in a converged width over long time, suggesting that the pushed wave profile enables the migratory population with diversity to keep in a tight shape.
source: In addition, we checked that the width of the entire group maintains in a converged width over long time, suggesting that the pushed wave profile enables the migratory population with diversity to keep in a tight shape (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Under a constant perceived gradient, each subpopulation migrates in different group speeds, suggesting a compact group migration of diverse population cannot be maintained.
source: However, as the drift velocity would vary by the chemotactic ability, each subpopulation migrates in different group speeds, suggesting a compact group migration of diverse population cannot be maintained in a constant perceived gradient (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When imposed to a spatially increasing driving force (a pulled wave), individual cells display super-diffusion processes and the density profile easily diverges.
source: In the latter case, when imposed to a spatially increasing driving force (a pulled wave, by definition), individual cells display super-diffusion processes. The density profile easily diverges in this case (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The pushed wave front, driven by a decreasing shape of driving force, enables a spatially ordered and compact pattern of phenotypes while on the move.
source: Therefore, we concluded that the pushed wave front, driven by a decreasing shape of driving force, enables a spatially ordered and compact pattern of phenotypes while on the move.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the model comparisons.

claim: A dense band of migrating cells that follow a self-generated moving chemoattractant gradient via consumption were recaptured as experiments.
source: As a result, a dense band of migrating cells that follow a self-generated moving chemoattractant gradient via consumption were recaptured as experiments (Appendix 1—figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 6A.

claim: The phenotypes were spatially ordered as χ varies.
source: The phenotypes were spatially ordered as χ varies (Appendix 1—figure 6B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 6B.

claim: The velocity profile of each phenotype decreases from the back to front as predicted by the OU-type model.
source: and the velocity profile of each phenotype decreases from the back to front (Appendix 1—figure 6C) as predicted by the OU-type model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 6C.

claim: Cells of each phenotype perform sub-diffusion, whereby the MSD along the migration coordinate relative to the group was bound at a level negatively correlated to χ.
source: As a result, cells of each phenotype perform sub-diffusion, whereby the MSD along the migration coordinate relative to the group was bound at a level negatively correlated to χ (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The width of the density distribution decreased with the reversion rate, as an approximate linear function.
source: The width of the density distribution, as an effect of the reversion force, decreased with the reversion rate, as an approximate linear function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The chemotaxis ability of bacteria was determined by the expression level of Tar.
source: In the experiments, the expression level of Tar (a chemoattractant receptor protein) was titrated by the concentration of external inducer (aTc). The chemotactic ability χ of bacteria was then determined by the expression level of Tar (Adler, 1969).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 4 caption and supported by citation.

claim: The chemotaxis ability increases with aTc concentration.
source: Using the migration speed of the bacterial range expansion to quantify the chemotaxis ability of the titrated strains, we found that the chemotaxis ability increases with aTc concentration (see Materials and methods and Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: As the Tar expression level (chemotactic ability) increased, the slope of the decreasing pattern increased.
source: More importantly, as the Tar expression level (chemotactic ability) increased, the slope of the decreasing pattern increased, which was consistent with the model prediction shown in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and compared with model predictions.

claim: The intersections between VD,i(z) and VG, as well as the peak positions and mean positions of each Tar-titrated density profile, shifted toward the front as the chemotactic ability increased.
source: The intersections between VD,i(z) and VG , as well as the peak positions and mean positions of each Tar-titrated density profile (Figure 4C), shifted toward the front as the chemotactic ability increased (as measured by the migration rate on agar plates; Cremer et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The VD cross point was always behind the peak position and the mean position, suggesting that cells were leaking behind.
source: The VD cross point was always behind the peak position and the mean position (Figure 4C), suggesting that cells were leaking behind.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The width of each Tar-titrated density profile (defined by 2σi) decreased as the reversion rate ri increased.
source: Moreover, the width of each Tar-titrated density profile (defined by 2σi) decreased as the reversion rate ri increased (Figure 4D), consistent with the model results in Figure 3C.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The width of the density profile is controlled by the reversion rate determined by the chemotactic ability χi.
source: Thus, as the OU-type model predicts, the width of the density profile is controlled by the reversion rate determined by the chemotactic ability χi .
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The collective consumption of attractant by bacterial group generates a spatial structure of individual drift velocity along the migrating group profile.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that the collective consumption of attractant by bacterial group generates a spatial structure of individual drift velocity along the migrating group profile.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Such a spatial profile of drift velocity results a pushed wave front on population level, and maintains diverse phenotypes in a compact migration group.
source: Such a spatial profile of drift velocity results a pushed wave front on population level, and maintains diverse phenotypes in a compact migration group.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: This pushed wave front enables spatial modulation of individuals to perform mean reverting random motions around centers sequentially aligned by their chemotactic abilities, thereby giving rise to a spatially ordered pattern.
source: Moreover, this pushed wave front enables spatial modulation of individuals to perform mean reverting random motions around centers sequentially aligned by their chemotactic abilities, thereby giving rise to a spatially ordered pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The population order could emerge among diverse individuals that following the same rule of behavioral modulation.
source: Therefore, we demonstrated that the population order could emerge among diverse individuals that following the same rule of behavioral modulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: This strategy of self-organization does not require sophisticated communications nor other hydrodynamic interactions among individuals.
source: This strategy of self-organization does not require sophisticated communications (Curatolo et al., 2020; Karig et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2011; Payne et al., 2013) nor other hydrodynamic interactions (Chen et al., 2017; Drescher et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010) among individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The observation of the decreasing drift velocity can imply the effective perceived gradient that cells experience.
source: Our observation of the decreasing drift velocity can imply the effective perceived gradient that cells experience.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: The spatial profile of drift velocity is mainly contributed by the consumption of the chemoattractant.
source: We believe that this spatial profile is mainly contributed by the consumption of the chemoattractant.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: The Tar-only strain (UU1624) could generate a stable group migration in the experimental condition similar to the wild-type strain.
source: By using a Tar-only strain (UU1624) (Gosink et al., 2006), we demonstrated that the mutant could also generate a stable group migration in our experimental condition similar to the wild-type strain (Appendix 1—figure 9G).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 9G.

claim: The secretion of self-attractants is unlikely a necessary condition of collective group migration.
source: This further suggests that the secretion of self-attractants is unlikely a necessary condition of collective group migration (Cremer et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2018; Keller and Segel, 1971a), although there are doubts about the existence of self-attractants in high density (Budrene and Berg, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The spatially dependent drift velocity provides a structured driving force of a migration group, resulting a pushed wave front.
source: The spatially dependent drift velocity provides a structured driving force of a migration group, resulting a pushed wave front.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary.

claim: Pushed and pulled waves are determined by the spatial distribution of the spreading velocity of a propagation front.
source: Pushed and pulled waves are determined by the spatial distribution of the spreading velocity of a propagation front (van Saarloos, 2003; Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: By direct measurement of drift velocity on single-cell level, we identified the chemotactic migration group of bacteria as a pushed wave.
source: Here, by direct measurement of drift velocity on single-cell level, we identified the chemotactic migration group of bacteria as a pushed wave.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The spatially decreasing profile of driving force does not only cause an ordered pattern of phenotypes, but also results a pushed wave front that enables a negative feedback control on the propagating speed.
source: The spatially decreasing profile of driving force does not only cause an ordered pattern of phenotypes, but also results a pushed wave front that enables a negative feedback control on the propagating speed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: This further allows a compact density profile for heterogenous population to migrate at the collective level.
source: This further allows a compact density profile for heterogenous population to migrate at the collective level.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: The advantageous to keep diversity in the pushed wave front was also reported in the growth-driven range expansion system.
source: The advantageous to keep diversity in the pushed wave front was also reported in the growth-driven range expansion system (Birzu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: The direct modulation of individual drift velocity in space could also maintain diversity in range expansion.
source: Our study revealed that, other than spatial regulation of fitness, the direct modulation of individual drift velocity in space could also maintain diversity in range expansion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: Cells could skip the potential wells from the back because the 'driving force' decreased again at the far back of the group.
source: However, it is noteworthy that cells could skip the potential wells from the back because the 'driving force' decreased again at the far back of the group (Long, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: This results in leakage of cells in the migratory group.
source: This results in leakage of cells in the migratory group (Holz and Chen, 1978; Novickcohen and Segel, 1984; Scribner et al., 1974).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Phenotypes with weaker chemotactic abilities were located at the back of the group, where the effective potential well was shallower, allowing for more chances to skip.
source: Phenotypes with weaker chemotactic abilities were located at the back of the group, where the effective potential well was shallower (Figure 3C), allowing for more chances to skip.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Such collective migration selects bacteria with higher chemotactic abilities.
source: Thus, such collective migration selects bacteria with higher chemotactic abilities (Liu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The simple computational principle of behavioral modulation to allocate different phenotypes in the collective group is likely not limited to sensing the self-generated signal by consumption of attractant.
source: The simple computational principle of behavioral modulation to allocate different phenotypes in the collective group is likely not limited to sensing the self-generated signal by consumption of attractant.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.

claim: Individuals tracing the accumulated signal secreted by all participants can reproduce similar spatial-temporal dynamics of behavioral modulation, as well as ordered arrangements of phenotypes in the migratory group.
source: A prominent example of trail-following migration (Couzin and Krause, 2003; Helbing et al., 1997) and a typical class of collective behavior is represented by a modified Langevin-type model, where individuals tracing the accumulated signal secreted by all participants (Equation S20) can reproduce similar spatial-temporal dynamics of behavioral modulation, as well as ordered arrangements of phenotypes in the migratory group (Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Appendix 1—figure 10.

claim: This mechanism of matching individual abilities by the signal strength might provide an explanation of how other higher organisms organize ordered structures during group migration.
source: Thus, this mechanism of matching individual abilities by the signal strength might provide an explanation of how other higher organisms organize ordered structures during group migration.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.
